text: LaserDisc (LD) was the first commercial optical disc storage medium and a home video format developed jointly by Philips, Pioneer, and movie studio MCA. Initially marketed in the United States in 1978 as MCA DiscoVision, the format was later rebranded as LaserVision by Pioneer, who took a leading role in its development and promotion. The term LaserDisc originally referred to Pioneer's player line but gradually became a generic term for the format itself, resulting in a genericized trademark. Standard LaserDiscs measure 300 millimeters (11.8 inches) in diameter, similar in size to a 12-inch (305 mm) phonograph record. Each disc consists of two single-sided aluminum platters bonded with plastic, with data stored via tiny pits and lands etched onto the surface. Unlike later digital optical formats, LaserDisc stores analog video using a composite signal, offering approximately 425 to 440 horizontal lines of resolution—nearly double that of VHS and Betamax and approaching DVD quality. It was the first home video format to support surround sound, with early titles featuring analog stereo audio and later versions including CD-quality digital audio using pulse-code modulation (PCM), as well as digital surround sound formats like Dolby Digital and DTS. Digital audio tracks were encoded by combining the baseband signal with FM-modulated video and analog audio carriers, resulting in a square wave pattern recorded as pits and lands. Audio carriers were placed at 2.3 and 2.8 MHz on NTSC discs to minimize visual interference, with the 2.8 MHz channel near the chroma signal requiring careful mastering to avoid beat interference. Pioneer implemented CX Noise Reduction on analog tracks, reducing dynamic range and peak levels to improve signal-to-noise ratio and reduce visible audio beats. NTSC discs could carry stereo analog and stereo PCM digital audio tracks (16-bit, 44.1 kHz), while PAL discs had two audio tracks—either both analog or both digital—with digital tracks at the same specifications. In the UK, "LaserVision" refers to discs with analog sound and "LaserDisc" to those with digital audio. Dolby Digital and DTS were first introduced on LaserDisc, with Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace (1999) being among the first to feature 6.1 channel Dolby Digital EX Surround in Japan. These digital audio signals were stored in a frequency-modulated form within the analog audio track and required a player with an AC-3 RF output and an external demodulator to extract the signal, which was then decoded. Many high-end AV receivers included such demodulators in the 1990s, but they were removed as DVD popularity grew. DVD players output Dolby Digital in digital form and were incompatible with LaserDisc’s modulated RF signal. Outboard demodulators and converters were available to translate the RF signal into standard Dolby Digital or to convert it to 6-channel analog audio. DTS audio required only an S/PDIF connection to a DTS decoder, and on DTS discs, digital PCM audio was not available, so playback on non-DTS systems fell back to analog Dolby Surround or stereo tracks, sometimes with supplementary audio making the original soundtrack unavailable. Only one 5.1 surround sound option existed per disc—either Dolby Digital or DTS—requiring compatible players and receivers. The earliest players used gas helium–neon lasers (632.8 nm), but Pioneer introduced the first consumer solid-state player, the LD-700, in March 1984, which also loaded from the front. Hitachi had introduced an industrial diode-based player earlier, but it had poor picture quality and was produced in limited numbers. After the LD-700, gas lasers were phased out in consumer players, though Philips continued using them in industrial units until 1985. Most players required manual disc flipping, though some diode-based models automatically flipped the disc. Pioneer produced multi-disc models holding over 50 discs, and briefly in 1984, a "LaserStack" unit added multi-disc capability to existing players like the Pioneer LD-600 or LD-1100, holding up to 10 discs and changing sides in about 15 seconds. The first mass-produced industrial player was the MCA DiscoVision PR-7820, later rebranded as the Pioneer PR7820, used in General Motors dealerships for training and car presentations. Most players made after the mid-1980s could also play Compact Discs, with a 4.7-inch indentation in the tray for CD insertion; some models like the CLD-M301 and CLD-M90 also functioned as CD changers. The Pioneer DVL-9, released in 1996, was both Pioneer’s first consumer DVD player and the first combination DVD/LD player. The Pioneer HLD-X0 was the first high-definition video player, with the HLD-X9 featuring a superior comb filter and dual laser diodes on the disc. MCA referred to the format internally as the Optical Videodisc System, Reflective Optical Videodisc, or Laser Optical Videodisc, and renamed it Disco-Vision in 1969, later changing to DiscoVision (without the hyphen) in 1978. MCA manufactured and distributed films under the "MCA DiscoVision" label, with the first release being the Jaws disc on December 11, 1978. Philips preferred the name "VLP" (Video Long-Play), with the Magnavox VH-8000 featuring the VLP logo; they briefly considered an audio-only format called "ALP" but abandoned it as the Compact Disc project became incompatible. The format was commercially introduced on December 11, 1978, in Atlanta, Georgia, two years after VHS and four years before the CD. The first LaserDisc title released in North America was the MCA DiscoVision edition of Jaws on December 15, 1978. Philips produced the players and MCA manufactured the discs, but the partnership failed and was dissolved. Pioneer acquired a majority stake in 1980 and began marketing the format as LaserVision and LaserDisc. Pioneer's LaserDisc players debuted in Japan in October 1981. By 1984, Philips and Sony introduced LV-ROM, a digital data format with a capacity of 3.28 GB, foreshadowing CD-ROM and DVD-ROM. Despite its superior audiovisual quality, LaserDisc failed to achieve widespread adoption in North America and Europe due to high player costs and lack of recording capability. It was more popular in Japan and wealthier parts of Southeast Asia, including Singapore and Malaysia, and became the dominant rental video format in Hong Kong during the 1990s. Market penetration reached about 10% of Japanese households by 1999 and about 2% of U.S. households (roughly two million) by the late 1990s. As of 2021, a small collector community remains in the United States and Japan. In Europe, the format remained obscure, though it saw limited institutional use, including the BBC’s use of LaserDisc in the mid-1980s for the Domesday Project and for broadcasting television idents from the early 1990s through the late 1990s using Sony’s CRVdisc variant. The last LaserDisc title released in North America was Paramount’s Bringing Out the Dead on October 3, 2000, and in Japan, new titles continued until September 21, 2001, with the final film being Tokyo Raiders from Golden Harvest. The last known LaserDisc release was Onta Station vol. 1018, a karaoke title issued exclusively in Japan on March 21, 2007. Pioneer ceased production of LaserDisc players in July 2009 and continued offering maintenance services until September 30, 2020, when parts inventory was exhausted. A total of 16.8 million LaserDisc players were sold worldwide, including 9.5 million by Pioneer. The format was largely supplanted by DVD by the early 2000s.

MCA first used the name Disco-Vision in 1969 and then again in 1978 with the name DiscoVision (without the hyphen), which became the official spelling. Technical documents and brochures from MCA Disco-Vision during the early and mid-1970s referred to the pressed discs as "Disco-Vision Records." MCA owned the largest film catalog in the world at the time and manufactured and distributed DiscoVision film releases under the "MCA DiscoVision" software and manufacturing label, with consumer sales beginning on December 11, 1978, starting with the film *Jaws*. Philips preferred the name "VLP," derived from the Dutch "Video Langspeel-Plaat," meaning "Video long-play disc," which in English-speaking countries was interpreted as "Video Long-Play." The first consumer player, the Magnavox VH-8000, featured the VLP logo. In the early and mid-1970s, Philips briefly considered an audio-only format called "ALP," which was later abandoned as the Compact Disc project became non-compatible within Philips. Until early 1980, the format had no official name. The LaserVision Association, composed of MCA, Universal-Pioneer, IBM, and Philips/Magnavox, was formed to standardize technical specifications and officially named the system "LaserVision." After its introduction in Japan in 1981, the format was launched in Europe in 1983 under the name LaserVision, though Philips used "VLP" in model designations like VLP-600. Sales in Europe were lackluster (around 12–15,000 units), prompting Philips to relaunch the format as "CD-Video" in 1987, using the name on both new 12 cm hybrid discs and standard 20 and 30 cm LaserDiscs with digital audio. While the "CD-Video" name and logo appeared on players and labels for years, the official name remained LaserVision. In the early 1990s, the format's name was changed to LaserDisc. Pioneer Electronics entered the optical disc market in 1977 as a 50/50 joint venture with MCA, producing MCA-designed industrial players under the MCA DiscoVision name (such as the PR-7800 and PR-7820). The 1980 launch of the VP-1000 player was noted as a "laser disc player," with the "LaserDisc" logo clearly displayed. In 1981, "LaserDisc" was used exclusively for the medium, though the official name was "LaserVision," as seen at the beginning of many releases. Pioneer reminded video magazines and stores in 1984 that "LaserDisc" was a trademarked term for LaserVision products manufactured by Pioneer Video or Pioneer Electronics. A 1984 Ray Charles ad for the LD-700 player used the phrase "Pioneer LaserDisc brand videodisc player." From 1981 until the early 1990s, all properly licensed discs carried the LaserVision name and logo, even Pioneer Artists titles. On single-sided Pioneer LaserDiscs, playing the wrong side caused a still screen with a happy, upside-down turtle having a LaserDisc for its belly (nicknamed the "LaserDisc Turtle"), with the text "Program material is recorded on the other side of this disc" below it, also appearing in Japanese on Japanese releases. MCA also manufactured discs for other companies like Paramount, Disney, and Warner Bros., sometimes adding their names to the disc jackets to indicate ownership. After DiscoVision Associates closed in early 1982, Universal Studio's videodisc software label (called MCA Videodisc until 1984) began reissuing DiscoVision titles. Many of these reissues, such as *Battlestar Galactica* and *Jaws*, were time-compressed versions of original CAV or CLV DiscoVision releases. The time-compressed CLV reissue of *Jaws* lacked the original soundtrack, replacing incidental background music due to high licensing costs (the original music was not available until the THX LaserDisc box set in 1995). The 1981 Universal/Columbia co-production *The Electric Horseman*, released in both CAV and CLV versions by MCA DiscoVision, remains unavailable in any other home video format with its original score intact; even the most recent DVD release has substantial music replacements. An MCA release of *Howard the Duck* shows only the start credits in widescreen before switching to 4:3 for the rest of the film, the only disc-based release until widescreen DVD formats with extras were introduced. The 1989 and 1996 LaserDisc releases of *E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial* are the only formats to include the cut scene where Harrison Ford, as the school principal, reprimands Elliott for letting frogs free in biology class. LaserDisc had several advantages over VHS: it offered a sharper picture with 425 TVL (NTSC) or 440 TVL (PAL) horizontal resolution compared to VHS's 240 TVL (NTSC), and Super VHS (1987) reduced the quality gap in luma resolution but retained low chroma resolution (about 40 TVL) versus LaserDisc's 70 TVL. LaserDisc supported both analog and digital audio, while VHS was mostly analog (with rare PCM in professional use), and NTSC discs could store multiple audio tracks, enabling features like director's commentaries and "Special Edition" releases. Disc access was random and chapter-based, like DVD, allowing quick jumps to any point, unlike VHS, which required rewinding and fast-forwarding. Initially, LaserDiscs were cheaper to manufacture than VHS tapes because they lacked moving parts and a plastic shell, with a single disc having five to six layers versus VHS's 14 parts. A disc could be stamped in seconds, while tape duplication required complex, time-consuming mechanisms. By the end of the 1980s, average disc-pressing prices exceeded $5.00 per two-sided disc due to plastic use and glass-mastering costs, while by the early 1990s, VHS tapes cost as little as $1.00. LaserDiscs had a longer potential lifespan than VHS tapes because they were read optically, avoiding physical contact that wore down magnetic tape. VHS tapes, with their magnetic coating in contact with spinning heads, suffered progressive wear and were fragile, easily damaged by creasing, stretching, or breaking. LaserDiscs were composite video formats, transmitting luminance and chrominance in one signal, which could not be fully separated due to comb filter limitations, unlike DVD's discrete YCbCr format, which provided higher fidelity, especially in high-contrast or moving scenes. LaserDiscs used analog video and were not digitally encoded or compressed, making them immune to video macroblocking or contrast banding, which could occur in DVD's MPEG-2 encoding. Early DVD releases often matched or sometimes surpassed LaserDisc quality, though some LaserDisc versions were preferred. DVDs used compressed audio like Dolby Digital and DTS, while most LaserDiscs had stereo (often Dolby Surround) CD-quality 16-bit/44.1 kHz tracks and analog audio. DTS-encoded LaserDiscs had 1,235 kbit/s soundtracks, compared to DVDs' 768 kbit/s. LaserDisc players offered greater control over playback, with pause, fast-forward, and fast-reverse commands always accepted, unlike some DVD players where content protection codes blocked such actions. With CAV discs, users could jump directly to any frame by entering the frame number on the remote, a feature not common in DVD players. Some DVD players had a cache feature that stored video in RAM, allowing frame-level access similar to LaserDisc. Damaged spots on LaserDiscs could be played through or skipped, while DVDs often became unplayable past damage; newer DVD players used repair+skip algorithms to continue playback, filling gaps with blank space or frozen frames. LaserDisc players recovered from errors faster than DVD players. Some videophiles argued that LaserDisc provided a "smoother," more "film-like" image compared to DVD, especially early DVD demo discs with encoding issues. LaserDisc had a lower video signal-to-noise ratio and bandwidth than DVDs, making DVDs appear sharper. Anti-piracy technology like Macrovision Copyguard could not be applied to LaserDisc due to the use of the vertical blanking interval for timecode, frame coding, and player control. Due to its small market share, the industry did not redesign the format to include such protection, which was later incorporated into DVD. LaserDisc supported multiple audio tracks, enabling extensive supplemental content and making it the first format to offer "Special Edition" releases; the 1984 Criterion Collection edition of *Citizen Kane* is credited as the first such release, setting the standard for future editions, including the first film with an audio commentary track, *King Kong*. Despite advantages over VHS and Betamax, LaserDiscs were heavy (about 250 grams or 8.8 oz), cumbersome, and prone to damage if mishandled. They required more mechanical effort to spin, generating more noise. The analog video signal limited playback time to 30/36 minutes (CAV) or 60/64 minutes (CLV) per side due to hardware manufacturers refusing to reduce line count or bandwidth, unlike VHS, which reduced bandwidth for longer playtime. After one side ended, the disc had to be flipped over, and some films required two or more discs. Many players, especially those built after the mid-1980s, could automatically flip discs, but this caused a pause during the switch. If a film exceeded two sides, manual swapping was required (except for the Pioneer LD-W1, which could load two discs and play each side of one before switching to the other). Perfect still frames and random access were limited to expensive CAV discs (30 minutes per side), though later models used digital memory buffers to access frames from CLV discs. LaserDiscs lacked built-in error correction, so dust or scratches could cause glitches, streaks, bursts of static, or picture interruptions. In contrast, DVDs used digital MPEG-2 with built-in error correction, preserving signal integrity until physical damage prevented data reading. A problem known as "crosstalk" could occur when the optical pickup was misaligned, the disc was damaged or warped, or due to subtle speed changes in CLV playback, causing adjacent track data to be read, resulting in swirling "barber pole" or rolling static lines. CAV discs avoided crosstalk because rotational speed remained constant. If the player was misaligned or the disc faulty, issues like "laser lock" could occur, where the player read the same two fields repeatedly, causing a frozen image. Playback quality varied significantly between LaserDisc players, with major differences visible even on standard televisions, and high-end models offering substantial improvements through post-processing. In contrast, DVD players produced visually similar images across models. Many early LaserDiscs were poorly manufactured, with adhesive containing impurities that penetrated the lacquer layer and chemically attacked the reflective aluminum layer, degrading the recorded signal.

On most televisions, a given DVD player produces a picture that is visually indistinguishable from other units; differences in image quality only become noticeable on larger screens, and significant improvements are generally only achieved with expensive, high-end players that allow post-processing of the MPEG-2 stream during playback. In contrast, LaserDisc playback quality varied significantly depending on hardware, with major differences appearing between different makers and models, even on low- to mid-range televisions. High-quality equipment helped sustain demand and kept prices high: in the 1990s, notable players sold for between US$200 and over $1,000, while older, less desirable models could be found for as little as $25. Many early LaserDiscs had defective adhesive that penetrated the lacquer layer and chemically attacked the reflective aluminum layer, degrading the signal—a problem known as "laser rot" among enthusiasts (internally called "color flash" by pressing plants). This could manifest as black spots resembling mold or burned plastic, causing skipping and excessive speckling, though rotted discs often appeared visually intact. Similar issues affected later optical standards, including a defective batch of CDs made by Philips-DuPont Optical in Blackburn, Lancashire, England, during the late 1980s/early 1990s. LaserDisc had limited market penetration in North America due to high player and disc costs—more expensive than VHS—and confusion with the inferior CED (Videodisc) format; despite this, it gained a following among videophiles for superior audio and video quality, reaching nearly one million American homes by the end of 1990. It was more popular in Japan, where prices were kept low to match VHS costs, enabling rapid adoption and making it the dominant consumer video format there. Anime collectors globally embraced LaserDisc for its high video and sound quality and availability of titles not on VHS, especially encouraged by Pioneer's in-house anime productions. In affluent Southeast Asian regions like Singapore, LaserDiscs were favored over videocassettes due to their durability in humid conditions and integration with the Japanese export market. In Hong Kong during the 1990s, before VCDs and DVDs, LaserDiscs saw high rental demand despite being priced around US$100 each, helping expand the video rental industry. NTSC LaserDiscs were used in Hong Kong due to integration with the Japanese export market, contrasting with the local PAL broadcast standard, creating a need for multi-system TVs and VCRs capable of handling both NTSC and PAL (and SECAM, though never popular in Hong Kong). Some players could convert NTSC signals to PAL for compatibility. Manufacturers never marketed recordable LaserDisc devices to consumers, despite VCRs offering recording, which hurt sales. The format's poor adoption was further hindered by the large disc size, high costs of players and media, and lack of recording capability. By 1995, several companies began investing in DVD, recognizing LaserDisc's future was short-lived. At the 1996 VSDA Convention, executives expressed mixed views on whether DVD could replace LaserDisc. Public awareness of DVD grew throughout 1996, and sales of LaserDisc players declined noticeably by that year, though sales of LaserDisc titles remained relatively stable, partly due to DVD's delayed release around Labor Day 1996. Despite being replaced by DVD by the late 1990s, many LaserDisc titles remain highly sought after by movie enthusiasts—for example, Disney's Song of the South, unavailable in the US in any format, was released on LaserDisc in Japan. This is due to the availability of films exclusive to LaserDisc and supplementary content not found on later DVD versions. Until 2001, many titles were released on VHS, LaserDisc, and DVD in Japan. In the early 1980s, Philips created a computer-interface LaserDisc player called "professional." In 1985, Jasmine Multimedia developed LaserDisc jukeboxes featuring music videos from Michael Jackson, Duran Duran, and Cyndi Lauper, which could be used with PCs to display educational or archival content, such as scanned medieval manuscripts—considered an early form of CD-ROM. In the mid-1980s, Lucasfilm developed the EditDroid non-linear editing system using computer-controlled LaserDisc players. Instead of printing film dailies, processed negatives were assembled into 20-minute segments and mastered onto single-sided blank LaserDiscs, enabling easier selection and preparation of edit decision lists (EDLs). This was the only way film crews could preview their work before the advent of video assist. Only 24 EditDroid systems were built, though the technology influenced later designs. Later versions used multiple discs on a single spindle with multiple playback heads and electronics, allowing instant access to any point on a disc, eliminating the need for large racks of players. In 1986, a SCSI-equipped LaserDisc player connected to a BBC Master computer was used in the BBC Domesday Project. The device, called an LV-ROM, stored video and data in CAV format, with data encoded as a binary signal in the analog audio track. Each CAV frame could contain video/audio or video/binary data, but not both; data frames appeared blank when played as video. Using the ADFS hard disc format, each file started at a specific sector, effectively skipping video frames. If all 54,000 frames were used for data, an LV-ROM disc could hold 324 MB per side. The Domesday system included a genlock, enabling mixing of video clips, audio, and computer-generated graphics—used effectively for high-resolution photos and maps, which could be zoomed. In the 1980s, Digital Equipment Corporation developed the IVIS system for training and education in the U.S., with Decision Point, a management simulation, winning the Nebraska Video Disc Award in 1985. Apple's HyperCard allowed Mac users to create databases of slides, animation, video, and sound from LaserDiscs and build interfaces using software called LaserStacks. User-created "stacks" were widely shared, especially in education, where teachers used them to access art collections and biological processes. Voyager was a leading distributor. Commodore's 1992 AmigaVision system included device drivers for controlling LaserDisc players via a serial port, enabling video overlay with computer graphics and multimedia integration, years before it became common. Pioneer also produced computer-controlled units like the LD-V2000, which had an RS-232 serial connection and no front-panel controls except Open/Close, with automatic playback upon disc insertion. Under a U.S. military contract, Matrox developed a combination computer and LaserDisc player for instruction. The computer was a 286, the player only reading analog audio, and the unit weighed 43 lb (20 kg), with sturdy handles for lifting. The computer controlled the player via a 25-pin serial port and a proprietary ribbon cable; many were sold as surplus in the 1990s without software, but the unit can still be operated by connecting a serial cable directly. The format's random access enabled a new class of video arcade games, starting in 1983 with Sega's Astron Belt. Cinematronics and American Laser Games created interactive movies like Dragon's Lair and Space Ace using the random-access feature. Pioneer's Laseractive and Halcyon were home video game consoles using LaserDisc media. In 1991, several manufacturers announced Hi-Vision LD specifications, a system based on NHK's MUSE analog HDTV, offering high-definition 1,125-line (1,035 visible lines; Sony HDVS) video with a 16:9 aspect ratio. MUSE players could also play standard NTSC discs and outperformed non-MUSE players even with NTSC content. MUSE players used a red laser with a narrower wavelength, allowing them to read through scratches and mild disc rot that would stop other players, and eliminated crosstalk. To view MUSE discs, a MUSE decoder was required, with some TVs and set-top tuners including built-in decoders. Equipment prices were high, especially early HDTVs, which often exceeded US$10,000, and the market in Japan remained small. Players and discs were never officially sold in North America, though some distributors imported MUSE discs, including releases of Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Lawrence of Arabia, A League of Their Own, Bugsy, Close Encounters of the Third Kind, Bram Stoker's Dracula, and Chaplin, as well as documentaries like one on Formula One at Suzuka. LaserDisc players and discs compatible with the European HD-MAC HDTV standard were also developed. Picture discs feature artistic etching on one side, often resembling movie characters or logos, sometimes with colored plastic instead of clear material; however, the "picture" side could not contain data, so video was only on one side. These are rare in North America. Pioneer, a major supporter of the format, was deeply involved in Japan's karaoke industry, using LaserDiscs for music and graphics, a format known as LD-G. While other labels produced LD-G discs, the market lacked the competition seen today, as most have shifted to CD+G. With the release of 16:9 televisions in the early 1990s, Pioneer and Toshiba introduced Squeeze LDs—enhanced 16:9 widescreen discs. During video transfer, the movie was stored in an anamorphic "squeezed" format, stretching the image to fill the frame and reducing letterbox bars, providing a 33% greater vertical resolution than letterboxed versions. This method was used in anamorphic DVDs, but unlike DVD players, few LD players could unsqueeze the image for 4:3 TVs, causing distortion if played on such sets. Some 4:3 TVs, like the Sony WEGA series, could be set to unsqueeze. Since few people outside Japan owned 16:9 TVs, the market for these discs was limited. In the U.S., only promotional 16:9 titles were available, such as Unforgiven, Grumpy Old Men, The Fugitive, and Free Willy, offered with Toshiba 16:9 TVs. Japan had a different lineup, including Basic Instinct, Stargate, Terminator 2: Judgment Day, Showgirls, Cutthroat Island, and Cliffhanger. Terminator 2 was released twice in Squeeze LD, the second being THX certified and an improvement over the first. Several recordable variants were developed for professional use but never marketed to consumers. The Recordable Laser Videodisc (RLV), introduced by Optical Disc Corporation in 1984, was a write-once, read-many format compatible with standard players, distinguished by a red/purple dye layer. Sony's Component Recordable Video disc (CRVdisc) was another write-once, read-many format for professional use, housed in a protective caddy resembling an oversized floppy disk, used by the BBC for years to play idents. Pioneer's LaserRecorder, introduced in fall 1991, was a rewritable system for professional video production, using CAV mode and protective caddies, with discs holding 32 minutes per side and rated for up to one million record/erase cycles. The dual-laser design enabled real-time, frame-accurate non-linear editing, used in EditDroid. The system sold for about US$39,950 (equivalent to $89,516 in 2024), with blank discs priced at approximately US$1,295 (equivalent to $2,902 in 2024). The most common LaserDisc size was 30 cm (11.8 in), similar to a 12-inch LP vinyl record, allowing 30/36 minutes per side (CAV NTSC/PAL) or 60/64 minutes per side (CLV NTSC/PAL). Most programming was produced on these discs. Smaller 20 cm (7.9 in) discs, known as "EP"-sized LDs, allowed 20 minutes per side (CLV), were much rarer, especially in North America, and roughly the size of 45 rpm vinyl singles. These were often used for music video compilations, such as Bon Jovi's "Breakout" and Bananarama's "Video Singles," as well as in Japanese karaoke machines.

The most common LaserDisc size was 30 cm (11.8 in), similar in size to 12 in (30.5 cm) LP vinyl records, and supported either 30/36 minutes per side (CAV NTSC/PAL) or 60/64 minutes per side (CLV NTSC/PAL). The vast majority of LaserDisc programming was produced on this format. Smaller 20 cm (7.9 in) "EP"-sized discs, allowing 20 minutes per side (CLV), were much rarer, especially in North America, and roughly matched the size of 45 rpm (7 in (17.8 cm)) vinyl singles. These were commonly used for music video compilations, such as Bon Jovi's "Breakout" and Bananarama's "Video Singles," as well as Japanese karaoke machines. Additionally, 12 cm (4.7 in) "single"-style discs, known as CD Video (CD-V) discs or Video Single Discs (VSD), were produced and playable on LaserDisc players. CD-V, launched in the late 1980s, included up to five minutes of analog video content with a digital soundtrack (typically a music video) and up to 20 minutes of digital audio CD tracks. The 1989 release of David Bowie's Sound + Vision CD box set featured a CD-V video of "Ashes to Ashes," and standalone promo CD-Vs included the video along with audio tracks: "John, I'm Only Dancing," "Changes," and "The Supermen." Despite the similar name, CD Video is incompatible with the later all-digital Video CD (VCD) format and can only be played on LaserDisc players with CD-V capability or dedicated smaller disc players. CD-Vs saw brief global popularity before fading. In Europe, Philips used the "CD Video" name in the late 1980s to rebrand the entire LaserDisc system; some 20 and 30 cm discs were branded "CD Video," but these were standard LaserDiscs with digital soundtracks and no audio-only CD content. The VSD format was introduced in 1990 and was essentially identical to the 12 cm CD-V but without audio CD tracks, intended to be sold at a lower price. VSDs were popular only in Japan and other parts of Asia and were never fully introduced to the rest of the world.
